source: Ariely, Au, Bender, Budescu, Dietz, Gu, Wallsten, Zauberman (2000) The effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges (Exp 2, Prediction 3)
finding: First-hand check of the 'Ariely 2000 found no gain' claim. Averaging a person's own two replicated probability estimates did almost nothing. Averaging two different people's estimates gave a clear gain, even though the within-person and between-person correlations were nearly equal.
numbers: N=64 volunteers (16 per cell of a 2x2 design), 200 statements about US city populations, 400 trials in 4 blocks; the same city pairs came back in later blocks, so the repeat is separated by about 100 trials, not seconds. Within-person correlation of repeated estimates .66; between-person .57. Mean probability score (lower is better): individual .252, within-person average .250, between-person average .234 (all 'between' vs 'within' tests significant, df=31). Resolution index DI': .666 individual, .657 within, .732 between.
quote: averaging pairs of replicated estimates within-subjects has virtually no effect on the quality of the estimates
limits: Probability judgments of true/false statements, not numeric quantities. Overconfident sample. Dyads only (J=2). The paper offers two reasons it cannot separate: pairs of correlated values need many more than two to help, or within-person dependence has a form the correlation misses.
agent_relevance: Confirms from the source that for judged probabilities, two same-source judgments add almost nothing (PS .252 to .250). Treat verbalized confidences from one model the same way: averaging two is not worth a call unless samples are decorrelated. [Gap 8]

source: White and Antonakis (2013) Quantifying accuracy improvement in sets of pooled judgments: does dialectical bootstrapping work? (postprint + supplement)
finding: Reanalysis of Herzog and Hertwig's own data. Their bigger gain in the dialectical condition comes from a score that is tied to how often the second guess equals the first. With a score that is not tied to that, both conditions gain the same.
numbers: H&H data: 40 historical-date items, 101 people (50 dialectical, 51 control). H&H score Adiff: 0.046 (SE .008) dialectical vs 0.010 (.008) control, t(99)=3.12, p=.002. But second guess equal to first: 0.7% dialectical vs 20.2% control, t(99)=10.3; 29 of 51 control people had median Adiff of 0. Paired median absolute error R1 vs average: 130.9 to 125.8 (dialectical) and 130.5 to 125.4 (control); interaction F(1,99)=0.00, p=.98; d=0.38 vs 0.39. With the second control group added: interaction F(2,148)=1.11 p=.33 (normalized) and 0.00 (raw).
quote: Dialectical instructions are not needed to achieve the wisdom of many in one mind.
limits: One data set, one task type (dates), re-analysis only, not a new experiment; the original authors' 2014 reply was not opened. A short comment (3 pages plus supplement).
agent_relevance: Both instruction types give the same accuracy gain (about 5 years of median error) once the identical-answer confound is removed. The 'think why you were wrong' prompt buys more change, not more accuracy. Test any 'contrary second sample' arm with a measure that does not reward change for its own sake. [Gap 6, Gap 8]

source: OSF preprint, authors not recorded (2026) From inner diversity to outer crowds: how instructions reshape error structure before aggregation
finding: A 2026 descriptive reanalysis of the authors' earlier inner-crowd data sets. A repeated-estimation baseline gave near-zero net gain. Dialectical bootstrapping made crowd accuracy worse. A 'disagreeing perspective' instruction moved answers more but did not improve crowd accuracy on average. Mixed-instruction crowds did not beat the best single instruction at any group size.
numbers: Abstract text only (read through the OSF API); no per-dataset numbers were available. Claims: 'people in general' perspective improved one 20-item set but not a related 8-item set; dialectical bootstrapping 'worsens mean crowd accuracy'; mixed-instruction crowds 'do not outperform the best single-instruction baseline across group sizes'.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; abstract only; the authors say the data do not cleanly identify changes in dependence. It is a reanalysis by the same group that reported the earlier positive ensemble result, so it partly contradicts that group's own 2025 five-style ensemble paper.
agent_relevance: Weakens the case for 'force a different perspective' as a reliable booster. Item pool matters a lot. Keep the contrary-sample arm as a test, not as a default. [Gap 6, Gap 8]

source: OSF preprint, authors not recorded (2026) When one measure hides multiple mechanisms: interpreting accuracy, similarity and assimilation in psychological data
finding: A measurement paper that reanalyses inner-crowd, ideology and anchoring studies. It says squared-error and absolute-error scores mix two things: a shift of answers toward or away from the truth (position) and a change in spread (dispersion). Reporting only the folded score can hide, blur or reverse a conclusion.
numbers: Abstract text only (OSF API). No numbers available.
limits: Abstract only; preprint. Relevant as a warning, not as a measured effect.
agent_relevance: When we score resampling on numeric tasks, report bias and spread separately. A drop in MSE from lower spread is the crowd-within effect; a shift of the mean toward the answer is something else (an anchor change). [Gap 8]

source: Yu, Zhang, Wang, Wang, Li, Ji, Liu, Piccardi (2026) Diversity Combining for Multi-Path LLM Reasoning (saturation of self-consistency)
finding: Measured how many independent votes K same-model samples are worth. The correctness correlation between samples caps the effective sample size at 1/c. On GSM8K it was about 0.45 to 0.60, so a ceiling of roughly 1.7 to 2.2 independent votes however many samples you draw. K=32 reached 96 to 98 percent of that ceiling.
numbers: GSM8K, temperature 0.7, K in {4,8,16,32}, 5 seeds x 100 instances = 500 pooled per cell. Qwen2.5-7B: c=0.60 (Table 2; text c near 0.59), effective K 1.42/1.55/1.65/1.67 at K=4/8/16/32, ceiling 1/c=1.71, vote accuracy at K=32 81.9%. Llama-3.1-8B: c=0.53, effective K 1.55 to 1.94, vote 79.3%. Mistral-7B: c=0.45, effective K 1.71 to 2.13, ceiling 2.21, vote 42.4%. An independence (binomial) model predicted 100.0%, 99.9% and 20.6%, off by 18 to 24 points; a beta-binomial fit from a K=4 pilot predicted K=32 accuracy within 3.3 to 4.8 points. Other tasks at K=4 pilot: HotpotQA c=0.61, BoolQ c=0.79.
quote: the pairwise correlation of path correctness caps the design-effect effective sample size of the vote at a finite ceiling
limits: Small instruct models (0.5B to 32B), not current frontier or reasoning models. c is the Pearson correlation of correctness across questions, so it mixes shared item difficulty with true within-item dependence. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to the within-model lambda question for discrete tasks: a same-model vote is worth about 1.4 to 2.1 independent votes on math word problems, saturated by K=8 to 16. Plan for 2 effective votes from one model, not k. [Gap 1]

source: Yu et al. (2026) Diversity Combining for Multi-Path LLM Reasoning (prompt-template diversity, 12 benchmarks)
finding: Using K=8 structurally different prompt templates instead of one prompt lowered the correctness correlation in almost every cell, but the accuracy change was small and mixed in sign. Decorrelation was strongest on open-ended QA and weakest on math.
numbers: 5 models, 12 benchmarks, 6 task domains, 250 items per cell (5 seeds x 50). Correlation fell in 55 of 57 valid cells, mean change -38 percent. By task: QA about -67%, multiple-choice and commonsense -35 to -49%, code about -22%, math -9 to -29%. Math vs QA difference: Mann-Whitney p=5.0e-4 (n=10 per group). Accuracy difference prompt-template minus same-prompt: within +-4 points on average and mixed in sign across the six domains (appendix Table 8).
limits: Same preprint and single lab. Template quality was not equated: weaker templates can lower per-sample accuracy. Binary-collapsed correctness for open-ended tasks (F1 >= 0.5).
agent_relevance: Resolves part of the Naik-versus-Wang conflict: prompt variation does lower sample correlation, but because members get a bit worse the net accuracy gain is about zero on average. Keep prompt variation as a test arm; do not assume it beats plain sampling. [Gap 9]

source: Yu et al. (2026) Diversity Combining for Multi-Path LLM Reasoning (Adaptive-K from a K=4 pilot)
finding: A small pilot (K=4 samples, estimate c) predicts how many samples are worth drawing. The rule kept 96 to 103 percent of the K=32 vote accuracy at 25 to 44 percent of the cost.
numbers: Rule: stop when the marginal gain of one more sample falls below 2.5 percent. GSM8K pilots: Qwen-7B c=0.60 gives K=6; Llama-8B c=0.53 gives K=8; Mistral-7B c=0.45 gives K=10. HotpotQA and BoolQ rows also reported (n=300 each). Varying the threshold from 0.01 to 0.1 kept 97 to 101 percent accuracy on Qwen-7B GSM8K. Pilot cost is counted in the net-cost figure.
limits: Global c, not per-item. Small instruct models. Authors note the compute saving is nominal if pilots are not reused.
agent_relevance: A cheap per-task calibration (4 samples on a pilot set) is enough to set the sample budget. Suggests a G12-style budget rule driven by measured c, not by a fixed k. [Gap 1, Gap 3]

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) Think more or read more? A token-budget theory of reasoning with shared context (Table 8, error correlation)
finding: Measured same-model error correlation (agreement on the same wrong answer) for five small open models on four tasks. It was moderate to high everywhere, and it did not change with group size or with the token window. The effective number of independent votes is capped at 1/rho.
numbers: 500 questions per task (GSM8K, MATH500, MMLU-Pro 10-way, CSQA 5-way). Round-0 error correlation rho: Qwen2.5-7B GSM8K .35, MATH500 .68, MMLU-Pro .56, CSQA .58; Falcon3-7B .40/.64/.56/.50; Llama3.2-3B .41/.52/.43/.42; Gemma2-9B .57/.64/.66/.58; Gemma3-12B .65/.77/.63/.55. Re-estimating at 7 windows or any group size moved rho by at most .05. Cap n_eff <= 1/rho, so about 1.3 to 2.9 votes. Effective size n_eff = n / (1 + rho (n-1)).
limits: Models of 3B to 12B, short reasoning (GSM8K chains about 275 tokens). rho measures same-wrong-answer agreement, so it depends on how concentrated the wrong answers are. Preprint dated Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Second independent measurement of the lambda ceiling, using a different definition from d05, gives the same answer: 1.3 to 2.9 votes from one model. Hardest, most structured tasks (MATH500, rho .5 to .77) have the lowest ceiling. [Gap 1]

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) Think more or read more? (self-consistency vs debate vs one long chain, matched windows)
finding: At equal token windows, plain voting matched or beat debate in 93 percent of 980 settings. A single agent allowed a much longer chain gained nothing from the extra room because its chains stop on their own; a group of short samples beat it.
numbers: 980 matched (group size, window) settings, five open models, four tasks: self-consistency >= debate in 93%; significantly better in 57%, debate significantly better in 0.5%, 42.5% tied (paired bootstrap). Qwen2.5-7B GSM8K at windows 6k to 32k: margin debate minus SC -0.40 +-1.11, -0.27 +-0.46, -0.07 +-0.81, +0.67 +-1.22, +0.07 +-1.47, +0.20 +-0.53 (all inside seed s.d.). Single long chain (room 8192, saturates near 275 tokens on GSM8K, 533 to 540 on MMLU-Pro) vs group at matched tokens: Qwen GSM8K 88.9 vs 93.7, MMLU-Pro 49.5 vs 49.8; Falcon3 GSM8K 81.5 vs 91.4, MMLU-Pro 46.5 vs 55.3.
limits: 7B-class non-reasoning models. The long-chain arm is the model's natural chain, not a trained long-thinking model. The group in the long-CoT table is a debate group, with SC said to recover the same advantage.
agent_relevance: For small non-reasoning models, k short samples beat one long pass, and the curve is flat from a window near 6k. Does not test modern reasoning models. [Gap 2]

source: Nitarach (2026) Model capability dominates: inference-time optimization lessons from AIMO 3
finding: On 50 IMO-level problems, every prompt-level change to the voters failed to help. Temperature near 1.0 already gave the diversity there was. The model size gap (gpt-oss-120b vs 20b at equal N=8) was about 4 times bigger than any prompt trick. The paper claims error correlation is already 'near zero', but that estimator is an algebraic artifact (see limits).
numbers: gpt-oss-120b N=8: temperature 0.5 -> 38, 0.8 -> 40, 1.0 -> 39.3 (21-run mean), 1.2 -> 37 (of 50). Equal prompt mix at T=0.5 scored 36 vs 38 for plain T=0.5. gpt-oss-20b N=8 scored 31.0 vs 39.3 for 120b; 20b at N=32 scored 26 (per-attempt time shrank, per-attempt accuracy fell from 0.61 to 0.52). Best majority vote 42/50 vs pass@20 of 45.5. Reported per-problem rho-hat: 19 points, all negative, mean -0.122 for N>=7.
limits: Our check: the per-problem estimator reduces algebraically to exactly -1/(N-1) for every problem with 0<p-hat<1 (N=3 gives -0.5, N=8 gives -0.143, N=16 gives -0.067), which is exactly what the paper reports. So 'negative correlation' is not data and cannot show that errors are uncorrelated. Item difficulty varies across problems, so the usable correlation is the cross-problem one. Scores are on a 50-problem leaderboard with run-to-run noise of a few points. Single author.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the AIMO rho-hat. The empirical part holds: prompt-variant voters did not beat temperature sampling, and model strength mattered more than sampling tricks. [Gap 9, Gap 1]

source: Liu (2026) Two calls, two moments, and the vote-accuracy curve of repeated LLM inference
finding: Two samples per validation item are enough to bound how much voting can help. The gain from 3 votes is at most half the rate at which two calls disagree. If two calls almost never disagree, extra samples are wasted.
numbers: Binary tasks QQP and QNLI, 7-8B local models. Q04 (QQP, Llama 3.1-8B, T=2.0): single 65.48%, second Table 2 column 16.83% (header symbol lost in the PDF text; probably the correctness correlation); two-call Wald lower bound on 3-vote gain +0.70 points; observed 3-call gain +3.22 [1.70, 4.75], 1,024 draws (64.65 to 67.87). N05 (QNLI, Phi-4-mini): bound +0.72; observed +4.65 [3.38, 5.93] (76.50 to 81.15). Qwen2.5-7B at T=0.2: two calls disagree on about 0.6% of examples, so 3- and 5-vote gains are capped at +0.46 and +0.47; observed 5-vote gain at most 0.17 (QNLI) and 0.04 (QQP) across three temperatures. Pools: 45,406 QQP pairs and 72,414 QNLI examples.
limits: Binary labels only; independent calls with a common per-item success probability; the bound is for one model/prompt/sampler. Third-call checks reuse the first two calls so they do not test coverage independently. Preprint.
agent_relevance: This is the cheap spread test for G12: run 2 samples on a validation set; the disagreement rate caps the gain from more samples. Directly answers whether a 2-sample test predicts who gains, at dataset level. [Gap 3, Gap 1]

source: Liu (2026) Two calls, two moments (temperature and rank reversal)
finding: Raising temperature lowered both single-call accuracy and the correctness correlation, and turned a zero voting gain into a clear one. A model that was worse on one call overtook another after voting.
numbers: QQP, Llama: temperature 0.2 to 2.0 moved the 5-vote gain from -0.06 to +2.57 points. QNLI: Phi-4-mini at T=2.0 trailed Llama 3.1-8B at T=0.2 by 0.86 with one call but led by 1.04 after five votes. Qwen2.5-7B had the highest single-call accuracy in both tasks but the smallest voting gains.
limits: Binary tasks, small models, high temperatures that would be damaging on long reasoning. Differences of about one point.
agent_relevance: Single-call accuracy does not tell how much sampling helps. Pick sampling settings by accuracy at the intended vote count, not at one sample. [Gap 1, Gap 3]

source: Sharma and Chopra (2025) The sequential edge: inverse-entropy voting beats parallel self-consistency at matched compute
finding: At equal token budgets, letting each chain build on the previous one beat independent parallel chains in 43 of 45 settings, with very large gaps on AIME-2025. This is the opposite of the 'parallel voting is best' result in d14 and d09.
numbers: 5 open models (gpt-oss-20B/120B, Qwen3-30B/235B-Instruct-2507, Kimi-K2), AIME-2024, AIME-2025, GPQA-Diamond, 3/6/9 chains, 4096 tokens per chain, T=0.7. Wins 43 of 45 (95.6%). Example Qwen3-235B AIME-2025 6 chains 83.3 sequential vs 40.0 parallel in Table 1 (text says 76.7 vs 30.0 at the same cell, so the paper disagrees with itself). Parallel accuracy of this model stays near 40% from 3 to 9 chains. Inverse-entropy weighting beat majority by +0.5 to +3.4 in parallel.
limits: AIME has only 30 problems per year, GPQA-Diamond 198; no confidence intervals. The 4096-token cap may truncate independent chains while continuation chains see earlier work. Non-reasoning instruct models. Text/table inconsistency noted. Preprint from a small lab; not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: The one study that says refine-in-sequence beats independent samples at equal tokens. Treat as a hypothesis to test with a proper equal-token arm and a reasoning model, not as settled. [Gap 2, Gap 4]

source: Wang, Zhu, Saad-Falcon, Athiwaratkun, Wu, Wang, Song, Zhang, Dhingra, Zou (2025/2026) Rethinking inference-time scaling: efficiency limits and linguistic signals
finding: Across reasoning and non-reasoning models, simple majority voting beat more elaborate verifier-free methods (best-of-N, mixture of agents, sequential revisions, combined sequential and parallel). Non-reasoning models hit a floor that more samples did not lift. Reasoning models gained little from external loops.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-7B/72B, Llama-3.1-8B/3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 7B to 70B, QwQ-32B-Preview. Tasks MATH500, AIME 2024 (30 problems), GPQA. Result is shown in figures; I could not extract per-cell numbers from the text. Reasoning-truncation baseline: forcing the think block to stop dropped reasoning models to the floor of the non-reasoning ones.
limits: Figures only, so no exact numbers; I read the text claims. Open-weight models of 2024-25, not the latest. Several of the comparisons are by the same group.
agent_relevance: Supports the default of plain voting as the compute-efficient baseline, and warns that sequential revisions can add 'reasoning drift'. Counter-evidence to d13. [Gap 2]

source: Zeng, Cheng, Yin, Zhou, Qiu (2025) Revisiting the test-time scaling of o1-like models
finding: For long-thinking models (QwQ, R1-Distill, LIMO), longer answers were not more accurate: correct solutions were shorter than wrong ones for the same question. Sequential self-revision gave small gains that stopped after about 10 steps and made two models worse. Parallel sampling gave better coverage and scaled better.
numbers: Five samples per question sorted by length; the longest averaged about twice the shortest. Sequential revisions: accuracy fell steadily with more steps for QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B; it rose and then oscillated for R1-Distill-14B/32B and LIMO. Majority vote on AIME with R1-Distill-32b rose from about 59 to about 73 across 2 to 16 solutions (table text scrambled; pairing uncertain). 'Shortest majority vote' beat plain majority vote.
limits: Table text is scrambled in the PDF, so the exact vote figures are approximate. Math tasks only. Early 2025 models.
agent_relevance: For reasoning models: more thinking in one chain stops paying and can hurt; k independent chains with a vote still help. Supports spending extra budget on breadth, with a cap on chain length. [Gap 2]

source: Loo (2025/2026) Self-consistency is losing its edge: diminishing returns and rising costs in modern LLMs
finding: On two Gemini 2.5 models, sampling more reasoning paths gave tiny gains: they were near ceiling already. Flash-Lite got worse past about 15 samples on MATH-500.
numbers: HotpotQA, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite: +0.4 points from 1 to 20 samples at about 20x the tokens. MATH-500, Flash-Lite: gain up to about 10 samples then a small decline after 15. Gemini-2.5-Pro on MATH-500: 98% single pass, 99.2% at 3 samples, 99.6% at 15 samples (+1.6 points at about 15x cost). Sample counts 3, 5, 10, 15, 20.
limits: Number of questions not stated in the text I read; no confidence intervals, so differences of 0.4 to 1.6 points may be noise. An LLM aggregator, not plain majority, picked the final answer. Single author, curves read from figures.
agent_relevance: Shows the 'no spread to exploit' boundary on current models: at 98% single-pass accuracy, 15x tokens buys 1.6 points. Supports gating extra samples on a cheap sign of difficulty or disagreement. [Gap 2, Gap 3]

source: Kohli (2026) Nine judges, two effective votes: correlated errors undermine LLM evaluation panels
finding: Even nine different frontier models from seven families behaved like about two independent voters, and the panel was no better than its best member. Many items had all nine judges wrong, far above independence.
numbers: 3 NLI datasets (MNLI, SNLI, AlphaNLI), 100 human labels per item, about 1,000 items on MNLI. Kish effective size n_eff=2.18, 95% CI [2.07, 2.31], mean pairwise phi .391, independence ratio 24.2%. Panel accuracy 72.0% vs best judge 71.8% (MNLI); SNLI best 84.2% vs panel 77.7%; AlphaNLI 91.2% vs 88.7%. 290 items all nine correct, 51 (5.1%) all nine wrong (under independence fewer than 1). Condorcet gap 22.0 points [19.5, 24.1]; shared item difficulty explains only 6.8% of it. Items where all nine agreed: accuracy 90.9% (n=319) vs 99.99% predicted by independence.
quote: the 9 judges effectively provide only about 2 independent votes' worth of information
limits: Cross-model, not same-model, and NLI classification; labels are noisy by construction (100 annotations). But it is an upper bound for what same-model samples can do: if different models give 2.2 votes, one model gives less.
agent_relevance: Unanimity is not proof: about 9 percent of unanimous panel answers were wrong. Same-model samples will be at least this correlated. Do not rely on agreement alone to trust an answer. [Gap 7, Gap 1]

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs agree, are they right? Auditing self-consistency and cross-model agreement as confidence signals
finding: Measured how often a model's own samples agree on a wrong answer. Agreement predicted correctness only weakly, and was worst for the most consistent model, which was confidently wrong about half the time on high-agreement items.
numbers: 53 runners x K=50 samples, 265,000 samples, GPQA Diamond and AIME. Spearman correlation of agreement with majority-correctness 0.20 to 0.59, all positive. gpt-4.1 on GPQA: agreement C >= 0.8 on 77% of case-result entries; the majority answer was wrong in 48% of those (95% CI [.40, .56]); mean C=0.89, ECE 0.41, Brier 0.42 (CoT-mini ECE 0.22). On AIME gpt-4.1 ECE 0.30 at majority accuracy 0.17. For gpt-4.1 on GPQA, 28% of unique cases were confidently wrong for every runner and 50% for at least one. Exploratory Claude tiers (haiku-4.5, sonnet-4.6, opus-4.7) showed the same frontier over-confidence.
quote: a model can agree with itself, and different models can agree with each other, out of shared bias
limits: Runs produced by a graduate course cohort (participants shared a course context); one OpenAI model family plus an exploratory Claude check done by an agent; part of GPQA 'confidence' is positional (option-shuffle control). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct measure of the shared-bias limit: the rate of confident wrong majorities is high on hard multiple-choice items. A high-agreement answer from one model is not a check on its correctness. Needs an outside check for G5 and G12 routing. [Gap 7, Gap 3]

source: Wang, Hong, Bagci (2026) A decodability criterion predicts when hidden-state selection beats majority voting in LLMs
finding: Showed the failure of voting when the correct answer is the minority: with more samples, voting moves toward the wrong consensus. A learned correctness probe beat voting there.
numbers: OpenBioLLM on MedQA, subset where the correct answer is a minority of the pool (131 questions): majority vote 20.4% at N=1 falls to 6.0% at N=16, while hidden-state selection (CASE) rises from 20.4% to 47.3%. On hard questions the probe gain is +16.8 points at N=16, and on the minority-correct bin +41.3. On MATH-500 both Qwen2.5 models gained +8.1 (p=0.043) and +6.6 points at medium difficulty.
limits: The 'minority-correct' subset is chosen by outcome, so a fall of the vote toward zero is partly built in by the selection; do not read 20.4 to 6.0 as a general rate. Needs hidden states, which an API agent does not have. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Says what we already believe (G5): voting cannot fix a wrong modal answer. The part usable by an agent is the check on selection, not the probe. [Gap 7]

source: Sakai, Song, Larson (2026) When does delegation beat majority? A delegation-based aggregator for multi-sample LLM inference
finding: On MMLU-Pro with a small model sampled 128 times per question, plain majority was well below the oracle, and an aggregator that uses answer entropy and reasoning-embedding similarity won back about 38 percent of that gap. About a third of questions were near-unanimous.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B, T=1.5, 128 samples per question, MMLU-Pro test (12,032 questions). Majority 40.71% all, 28.00% on the 8,099 non-trivial questions; oracle (pass@16) 44.68% all and 33.93% non-trivial; best aggregator 42.21% and 30.24% (+2.24 points non-trivial, McNemar 366 wins vs 185 losses, p about 1e-14). Trivial questions (top letter gets >= 12 of 16 votes): 3,933 of 12,032, 32.7%.
limits: 1.7B model, multiple choice, high temperature. Gain is about 1.5 points overall. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Quantifies selection loss for a same-model pool: majority leaves about 4 to 6 points to the oracle, and a smarter combiner recovers a part. About one third of items have no spread to work with. [Gap 3, Gap 7]

source: Verma (2026) Try again, don't look back: blind resampling outperforms self-repair in small code models
finding: Retrying from a fresh prompt (no sight of the failed attempt) beat showing the model its own failed attempt, at equal retries, for models up to 3B and tied at 7B. Execution feedback added nothing over a content-free 'wrong' notice. Cause: anchoring on the previous attempt.
numbers: MBPP+, 1.5B/3B/7B, pass@1 at k=8 retries. 1.5B: blind resample .749 vs .688 for placebo, feedback and reflection (penalty 6.1 points, p=.006). 3B: resample .778, placebo .709, feedback .735, reflection .743. 7B: resample .820, placebo .802, feedback .810, reflection .828. Near-identical retry program (similarity > 0.95): 33 to 68% when shown its own code vs 2 to 14% for blind resampling. Similarity up 0.30 to 0.38. 46 to 53% of all attainable gain arrives by retry 2. Penalty tracks baseline quality (r=0.96 over 6 configurations, two families). Retrieved solutions from other tasks changed pass@1 by at most 3.5 points.
quote: Shown its own code, the model edits; asked afresh, it reconsiders.
limits: Small code models, pass@1 on one benchmark, pre-registered but a single author; not a numeric-estimation task. Placebo/feedback ordering not resolved by the anchoring measure.
agent_relevance: Closest measured analogue of delay: fresh context gave a lower similarity (2 to 14%) between samples than same-context continuation (33 to 68%). Supports the G2 rule that samples meant to be independent should not see earlier samples. [Gap 4]

source: Ferreira, Liu, Zheng (2026) Beyond symmetric agents: cognitive diversity and multi-agent debate in small language models
finding: A large controlled test of whether diversity (personas, temperature, model identity) is what makes debate work. It rejected the idea on every axis. Debate beat a single agent but tied or lost to equal-budget voting. Persona prompting cost accuracy. Mixed-model teams lost to votes over their own members.
numbers: 23 models from 11 vendor families, 5 tasks, 5,500+ runs, 100 problems per task. Debate vs solo: +3.3 (GSM8K), +6.6 (MMLU), +5.7 (CSQA) points. Debate vs 9-sample voting: no advantage; on CSQA sampling won by 2.3 points (p=.011); debate costs 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens. Mean accuracy over tasks (table text scrambled, row read as Solo 80.4, Debate 84.4, SC-9 84.8, Persona 81.9). Mixed-model debate minus matched vote over its own roster: -1.04 points, CI [-1.61, -0.52], 320 team-task cells. Nearly all debate gain comes in the first exchange. A hidden bug (debate transcripts overflowing context) changed the debate-vs-sampling gap from -1.8 to parity.
limits: Small open models (0.6B to 109B); 100 problems per task. Personas are not the same as a 'contrary second sample' prompt. Preprint.
agent_relevance: No sign that role or perspective prompts are better than plain resampling for small models: they pay a persona tax. Place the contrary-sample arm as a test with a plain-sample control at equal tokens. [Gap 6, Gap 9]

source: Bilal, Mohsin, Umer, Trigg, Subhan, Ali, Hougen (2026) Refining over resampling: test-time self-correction for LLM reasoning
finding: Independent samples repeat a few reasoning directions: unique reasoning clusters grew from about 1.2 at N=2 to about 2.5 at N=32 on AIME-24. Refining each sample (critique then correct) before voting beat voting over raw samples with small models.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Ministral-8B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B; AIME24/25, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500; N=8, depth up to 4. Average accuracy for Qwen2.5-1.5B: Maj@8 13.21% to 25.67% with refinement (compute-normalized gain 17.10); vs RM@8 14.95% to 25.67%. Qwen2.5-Math-7B improved over RM@8 by 2.36 points. AMC23 Qwen2.5-1.5B 25.0% to 32.5% vs best verifier baseline. Refined-rollout diversity stayed at 0.80 to 0.97 through depth 4.
limits: Not an equal-compute comparison: the authors say the main comparison fixes the sample count, not total FLOPs. Gains are largest for the weakest model and small for 7B math. Small test sets (AMC 40 problems, AIME 30). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports a second, weaker result: sample diversity saturates at about two clusters, so a refine-then-vote design may add value, but the claim needs an equal-token control. [Gap 2, Gap 4]

source: Halawi, Zhang, Wang, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models (Table 14, ensembling methods)
finding: Compared five ways to combine 6 same-system forecasts. All of the simple combiners were within 0.0007 Brier of each other. Only the LLM-as-aggregator (USC) was worse than no ensembling.
numbers: Validation set, 6 base reasonings per question. Brier: mean .1656, median .1651, geometric mean .1655, trimmed mean .1649, USC .1691, no-ensemble baseline .1676, human crowd .1600. The 'trimmed mean' here is nonstandard: halve the weight of the forecast farthest from the median.
limits: Validation set only; the baseline is the average member, so the gain is 0.0027 (1.6%) at best and is likely inside noise. The base reasonings differ in prompt and retrieval, not only in sampling noise.
agent_relevance: Combiner choice does not matter at n=6: mean, median and trimmed mean are equivalent. Use a plain median or mean, in code, and do not hand the combination to the model. [Gap 5]

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) Think more or read more? (self-refine tables 14 and 15)
finding: Letting a model re-read its own first draft (same context) gave small or no gains, and reading one peer answer did not reliably raise per-agent accuracy. Voting accounts for most of the debate gain.
numbers: Best-round self-refine gain over first draft (grid best): Qwen2.5-7B GSM8K 0.0, MATH500 1.3, MMLU-Pro 2.5, CSQA 1.1; Falcon3-7B 4.3, 3.5, 6.7, 0.7; Gemma-2-9B 2.0, 3.3, 3.2, 0.0; Gemma-3-12B 0.9, 2.3, 2.9, 0.2; Llama-3.2-3B 0.0 in all four. Loss at the tightest window up to 44.3 points. Reading one peer answer changed per-agent round-1 accuracy by -1.97 and -3.78 (Qwen2.5-7B) and +2.33 and +4.11 points (Falcon3-7B).
limits: Gains are oracle (best round per cell), so they are optimistic. 7B-class models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Same-context continuation is a weak way to get a second opinion (gain 0 to 6.7 points, often negative); a fresh draw is the baseline to beat. [Gap 4]

source: Harshavardhan (2026) Self-anchoring calibration drift in large language models
finding: Tested whether stated confidence drifts when a model builds on its own earlier answers across turns, versus independent repetition. Effects were model specific and mostly small, and near zero on factual items.
numbers: 3 frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2), 150 questions, three conditions (single turn, multi-turn self-anchoring, independent repetition). Claude: confidence change -0.032, t(14)=-2.43, p=.029, d=-0.627. GPT-5.2: +0.026 on open-ended items. Gemini: no significant change (t(14)=0.38, p=.710), but its calibration error fell from .327 to near zero with independent repeats and stayed flat at .333 when self-anchored.
limits: Weak design: each test has df=14 (15 units), results diverged from the pre-registered hypotheses, single author. The measured quantity is stated confidence, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Only weak support for the idea that same-context continuation reduces independence and calibration; do not rely on it. [Gap 4]
